analysis.one_liner: Sets binding deadlines for EPA to write water discharge limits and health standards for toxic PFAS chemicals.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 22 House members including three Republicans, was referred to a House committee and died there without ever receiving a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: PFAS ('forever chemicals') are long-lasting industrial chemicals linked to health problems, and they end up in rivers, lakes, and drinking water. This bill would force the EPA to set enforceable limits on how much PFAS a set of industries — chemical makers, plating shops, textile mills, landfills, tanneries, paint and plastics plants — may discharge into water, with hard deadlines starting in 2025. It would also require monitoring at airports and paper plants, make a standard PFAS test method official, and send $200 million a year to local water treatment plants to filter out PFAS. It never got past the committee stage.
analysis.who_benefits: People who drink tap water, swim in, or fish from lakes and rivers downstream of PFAS-discharging factories, and the local water utilities that currently bear the cost of removing PFAS that factories discharge upstream of them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People who drink tap water and fish

how_it_helps.text: Directs the EPA to publish human health water quality criteria for every measurable PFAS within three years of enactment [S2].

Orders final rules setting effluent (discharge) limits for chemical, electroplating, and metal finishing plants by mid-2025, textile mills and landfills by mid-2026, and tanneries, paint, and plastics plants by mid-2027, with monitoring required immediately [S2].
Requires the EPA to decide by the end of 2025 whether to write discharge limits for paper mills, airports, and electronics plants, and to publish any such limits by the end of 2027 [S2].

Authorizes $200 million per year, for five years, in grants to local publicly owned treatment works to run PFAS pretreatment and monitoring programs, so ratepayers are not the only ones paying to clean up industrial PFAS [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Industries that discharge PFAS into water — chemical manufacturers, metal platers, textile mills, tanneries, paint and plastics plants, and landfills — would bear the cost of monitoring, treatment, and compliance. Taxpayers would fund the grant program if Congress appropriates the money.
analysis.who_pays_short: PFAS-discharging factories and, for grants, taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs would fall on manufacturers, which could raise prices or shift production; the bill sets fixed statutory deadlines (starting mid-2025) that are faster than the EPA's usual rulemaking pace, leaving the agency little room if testing or treatment technology lags [S2].

The $200 million-a-year grant program for treatment plants is authorized but not actually funded — it is 'subject to the availability of appropriations,' so Congress would still have to vote the money, and water utilities could face monitoring and pretreatment obligations in the meantime [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — enforceable federal limits on industrial PFAS pollution reaching drinking water — is large and public, since PFAS do not break down and accumulate in water supplies and bodies. The main costs are real but ordinary for pollution regulation: industry compliance spending and potential price increases, plus the risk that the statutory deadlines outrun the EPA's technical capacity. On balance the bill's design is conventional Clean Water Act practice on a shortened clock.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in April 2024 and referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, which never acted on it, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Representative Chris Pappas introduced the bill on April 18, 2024, joined by Representatives Fitzpatrick, Kildee, and Posey as original cosponsors [S1].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, the only action it ever received [S4].
It gathered 22 cosponsors, including 3 Republicans, but never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or any Senate action before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Industries that discharge PFAS — chemical, plating, textile, tannery, paint, plastics, and landfill operators — avoided federal discharge limits, and the treatment-plant grant program never materialized.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan but lopsided: 19 of 22 cosponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-led committee never acted on the bill.

industries.industry: PFAS manufacturers and PFAS-using chemical plants (organic chemicals, plastics, synthetic fibers)
industries.note: The bill would have imposed binding discharge limits on these plants by mid-2025 and immediate monitoring. Its death leaves them free to discharge PFAS under no industry-specific federal limits.
Covered by the first wave of deadlines in the bill, which never took effect.

industries.industry: Textile mills, leather tanneries, paint formulators, and plastics molders
industries.note: Would have faced PFAS discharge limits by 2026-2027 under the bill; the deadlines died with it.

Utilities would have gained $200 million a year in grants for PFAS pretreatment, saving ratepayers money, but also would have gained new monitoring duties. With the bill dead, they keep bearing cleanup costs without dedicated federal funding.

industries.industry: Paper mills, airports, and electronics manufacturers
industries.note: The bill would have required monitoring and an EPA decision on future limits for these dischargers; nothing was ever required of them.
